prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene at magic angles and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle graphene, opening the field of moire quantum matter

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is the one candidate on the list where a simple, analysable mechanism and a decisive experiment are tied together in a single chain. The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model shows that interlayer tunnelling renormalises the Dirac velocity to zero at discrete angles, a clean statement that could be checked on paper before anyone built a device. The 2018 observation of correlated insulation and superconductivity then turned a prediction into a platform, and the platform has since been reproduced by many independent groups and spread to twisted TMDs, fractional Chern insulators and tunable correlated phases. This is exactly the combination of universal mechanism, experimental contact and a new subfield that I look for. The three names form a natural theory-plus-experiment configuration with no need to dilute it. Opening support is the strongest on the list (three first places among eight), but I rest the case on the science: the flat-band mechanism is understood even though the pairing mechanism is not, so the citation can be phrased around the platform and correlated phases rather than around an unresolved microscopic claim.
statement.case_against: The field is only about eight years old, and the microscopic origin of the superconductivity is unresolved, so a prize risks honouring a platform whose central physics is still in flux. Credit is also exposed: Yuan Cao and the other experimental co-leads, the Dean group's related moire work, and earlier twisted-bilayer theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) are outside the credited names, and I cannot verify the priority history from the supplied text. If colleagues judge that the committee's usual standard demands more consolidation, B053, which is more mature and equally conceptual, is the better choice.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks topological insulators first as a conceptual reclassification of band insulators with a clean theory-experiment chain through Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, though he flags the overlap with the 2016 prize and the missing Zhang, Bernevig and Hughes.
responses.response: I agree on the conceptual weight and I ranked it second with the same three names, so this is a narrow disagreement. My reservation is the credit gap you identify yourself: with the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that led to the HgTe experiment and Hasan's 3D photoemission both outside a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio, the citation cannot describe a single chain without an uncomfortable omission. The moire trio is tighter, since the prediction and the decisive experiment come from exactly the credited people. I do not think the 2016 overlap is decisive for B053, but it is a real discount that B015 does not carry. If the committee prefers maturity over cleanliness of attribution, I would move to B053.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first as a measurement-limited advance (1e-18 uncertainty, gravitational redshift sensing, redefinition of the second) with a clean two-person Katori-Ye credit, and treats it as the natural follow-on to the 2005 comb prize.
responses.response: The attribution is indeed the cleanest on the list and the maturity is not in question. My hesitation is about discovery content: I ranked it seventh because much of the post-2010 progress is the systematic refinement of a good idea, and the redefinition of the second has not happened, so the principal payoff may still lie ahead. I would also want the citation to say what is new in principle, the magic-wavelength condition, rather than a record accuracy that another group could surpass next year. I take your point that it is timely and I keep it as an alternative, but I do not think the maturity argument by itself outranks a platform that has created a new field of many-body physics.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as instrument-driven discovery of a new window, and treats the lattice clock as a close second on control of systematics, while noting the moire work is somewhat early and that he leans on colleagues for the condensed-matter detail.
responses.response: I share your weight on independent reproduction, and for moire graphene it is satisfied: correlated insulators and superconductivity have been reproduced by many groups across several material families. The place where I differ is IceCube. The diffuse flux is secure, but you yourself note that source identification rests on a few objects at roughly 3-4 sigma and that the credit among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the AMANDA lineage is unresolved. That is a less mature picture than the one for B015 and a harder three-person allocation, so I would keep it off my list until the source story firms up.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as a clean architecture underlying essentially all superconducting processors, while flagging the 2025 prize overlap, the omission of Girvin and Devoret, and his own proximity to the field.
responses.response: I value the strong-coupling physics, but I ranked it sixth because of exactly the issues you name. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits leaves little room for another circuit-centred award this soon, and the omission of Girvin (and the Huard and Devoret lineage) weakens a Blais-Wallraff-Schoelkopf trio. I also read the case as more technology-enabling architecture than new fundamental mechanism. I appreciate that you have declared your proximity to the field, and I would treat your ranking as expert information on what is conceptually new here, but I would not move it ahead of B015 or B053.

responses.point: Olsson ranks magic-angle graphene first as a clean experimental opening of a new platform, and ranks topological insulators second with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, crediting the decisive experiments as well as the foundational theory.
responses.response: We agree on the first choice and on the pairing of Bistritzer-MacDonald with Jarillo-Herrero. On B053 I would qualify your Kane-Molenkamp-Hasan set: replacing Mele with Hasan rewards the 3D experiment but separates Kane from his co-author on the founding quantum spin Hall papers, which I find hard to defend. If the committee goes to B053 I would keep Kane, Mele and Molenkamp for a 2D quantum spin Hall citation and treat Hasan's 3D work as a distinct step that cannot be honoured within three names.

uncertainties: Whether the priority of the flat-band prediction over earlier twisted-bilayer theory can be settled to the committee's satisfaction.
Whether eight years and an unresolved superconducting mechanism clear the committee's maturity standard for B015.
Whether Yuan Cao and the Dean group should enter the credit, and how that interacts with the three-person limit.
How much weight to give opening Borda points for B057 versus the discovery content of lattice clocks.
Whether a B053 prize should name Mele or Hasan alongside Kane and Molenkamp.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile: I have no collaboration with any credited candidate. I note only that Johansson and Olsson are in the Gothenburg physics environment, which is an institutional proximity rather than a scientific connection to any shortlisted discovery.
